title: Airport at 5 a.m.
synopsis: Your flight is in ninety minutes. The taxi smells like coffee and bad news.

nodes.text: Five in the morning and the cab smells like a coffee that was spilled during a previous administration. The driver's name is on the dash: Emeka. The radio is playing something with a walking bass at a volume that assumes agreement. He wants to know what is in the bag. Your flight leaves in ninety minutes.

choices.consequence: You say laptop, and by the second light he is telling you about his brother's restaurant and the man who controls the parking behind it.
You close your eyes against the window. He turns the jazz down two clicks, which is somehow more attentive than any conversation would have been.

nodes.text: At the on-ramp he does not take the on-ramp. He explains, without slowing down, that the highway at this hour is a trap involving three trucks and a bridge inspection, and that he knows a way through old downtown that nobody uses. He says nobody uses it a second time, and seems pleased with the phrasing.

choices.consequence: You tell him to go ahead, and he nods once, like a man who has been waiting since the airport for somebody to let him drive properly.
You ask for the highway and he takes the highway in silence, and the walking bass gets slightly louder in a way you cannot prove was deliberate.

nodes.text: A crane sits across both lanes of Delancey with its outriggers down and a man in a vest holding a sign that is not going to change. Emeka puts the car in park. He does not swear. He exhales through his nose for a long time and then informs the windshield that this crane was not here on Tuesday.

choices.consequence: You put cash on the console before the meter has finished and he tries to hand it back twice. You win, but not comfortably.
You get out at a red light with a laptop bag and jog four blocks in dress shoes while he rolls alongside the curb, shouting directions.

nodes.text: Forty minutes to gate. The security line has left the security area entirely and become a feature of the terminal architecture, doubling back past a currency exchange and a man selling neck pillows. A woman with a clipboard says it is moving. It is not moving. It has a texture, and the texture is stationary.

choices.consequence: You take the shorter line and end up behind a family with a stroller, a cello, and a small dog in a bag. The dog is calm. You are not.
You go straight to the desk, explain everything while breathing hard, and an agent named Denise decides to like you, which is the only reason any of this works.

nodes.text: Final boarding, and you reach B14 doing the particular run of a person who refuses to admit they are running. The agent scans your phone without looking up from her screen. On the jet bridge you pass a man who is clearly on your flight and clearly walking, and you hate him with the last available energy in your body.

choices.consequence: You apologize to 23B and 23C twice apiece, and 23B says it is fine in a tone carefully establishing that it is fine.
You sit, buckle, open a paperback, and hold it upside down for a page and a half before anything about that registers.

nodes.text: The sun comes up somewhere past the wing and the whole cabin turns orange for about four minutes. The bag is under the seat. The laptop is in the bag. Nobody has died, nothing has been left in the trunk of a cab in old downtown, and it is not yet six-thirty in the morning.

choices.consequence: You buy a coffee that costs more than the tip did and tastes worse than the cab smelled, and you drink every drop of it.
You are against the window before the seatbelt sign goes off and gone before the landing gear has finished folding away.

nodes.text: Emeka texts a week later to ask whether you made it. You did, you tell him. After that it is occasional: a photograph of his brother's restaurant, a link to something he wrote. He writes essays. They are about the city between four and six in the morning and they are, against every reasonable expectation, very good. You kept the one about the crane. You have read it more than once.

You land, you make the meeting, and the cab is gone from your head inside a week. The driver's name goes first, then the crane, then the exact dimensions of the disaster. What stays, oddly, is the jazz. A walking bass at five in the morning, turned down two clicks the moment you shut your eyes. You hear it in a hotel lobby years later and are, for a second, back in old downtown.
